results.summary:
White also retains its material grounding while acquiring aesthetic and ethical dimensions. In the final line of Hexagram 22, "White Adornment" signals an ideal of beauty stripped to its essentials. François Jullien interprets this "whiteness" as a form of blandness, valued for its

capacity to contain all potential differentiations without committing to anyone. \(^{287}\) The "white reeds" of Hexagram 28 similarly merge tangible materiality with moral clarity.  

Crimson, expressed through zhu (朱), denotes the cinnabar- dyed knee- covers worn by nobles, referenced in Hexagram 47. These garments possessed both material rarity and social exclusivity; the brilliance of cinnabar signalled authority and ritual privilege. The paired term fu (绫), referring to patterned or bicoloured sashes, further demonstrates how chromatic differentiation marked civilised refinement and ritual order.  

Archaeological manuscripts aligned with the Zhouyi tradition reinforce this chromatic logic. Warring States bamboo slips from the Shanghai Museum employ red and black marks to distinguish structural units, while silk manuscripts from Chu and early Han contexts show cinnabar lubricating used for headings and divisions. \(^{288}\) The manuscript evidence confirms that a dual- colour system structured the visual organization of early textual culture, reflecting practices deeply resonant with divinatory traditions.  

Thus, in Zhouyi, colour operates simultaneously as material descriptor, ritual code, and cosmological signifier. Xuan articulates Heaven's depth; Huang expresses ethical centrality; Bai conveys aesthetic restraint; and Zhu marks nobility and ritual authority. The chromatic system of Zhouyi is therefore multivalent, transforming hue into a grammar of meaning that structures ritual action, moral orientation, and cosmic order.

results.title: The Making of the Zhouyi through the Bamboo-Silk Manuscripts
results.summary:
#### 역류 출토문헌을 통한 고대 『주역』의 형성과 전개 The Making of the Zhouyi through the Bamboo-Silk Manuscripts

1충북대학교
...
이 연구는 출토문헌을 통하여 고대 『주역』의 형성과 전개 과정의 일면을 살펴보고자 하는 것이다. 그 방법으로 괘획, 괘서, 사상적 내용이라는 세 가지 측면에 중심을 두고 고찰하고자 한다. 첫째, 은상시기 출토자료의 역괘 및 전국시대 숫자괘들을 통해 숫자괘를 함부로 『주역』의 괘로 환원하여 설명할 수 없다는 것을 밝혔다. 또한 전국시대까지는 여전히 숫자괘를 사용하는 역점이 존재하고 있었으며, ‘’와 ‘━’의 두 가지 부호를 사용하는 『주역』과 함께 통용되고 있었다. 둘째, 상박초간 『주역』, 마왕퇴백서 『주역』, 청화간 『별괘』, 왕가대 『귀장』을 살펴보면 전국시대에는 『주역』의 괘서가 적어도 2종 이상 있었음을 알 수 있다. 이것이 결국 전한 문제 시기 이후 하나로 통일되어 전승되었다고 생각된다. 셋째, 마왕퇴백서 『역전』, 「이삼자문」과 「단전」 그리고 마왕퇴백서 『역전』, 「목화」의 내용을 분석하여 고대 『주역』의 양상을 살펴보았다. 「이삼자문」의 성립은 『순자』, 「非相」과의 비교를 통해 이미 『순자』 이후라는 것이 논증되었다. 따라서 「이삼자문」을 보다 발전시킨 논리를 지닌 「단전」은 전한 문제기 이후에 성립되었을 것이다. 마왕퇴백서 『역전』의 내용은 방대하며 하루아침에 성립되었다고 보기 어렵지만, 그 속에는 유가 사상을 중심으로 여러 제자백가의 사상이 융합되고 있다. 이 같은 종합적 저작이 한나라가 등장하자마자 갑자기 만들어졌다고 보는 것은 무리한 추정일 것이다. 오히려 전국시대 말기부터 서서히 형태를 잡아가고 있었다고 보는 것이 합리적일 것이다. 『역전』의 저술은 전국시대 말기부터 이루어지고 있었다.

This is to study formation and development of the Zhouyi through the Bamboo-Silk Manuscripts. The Zhouyi will be studied with at three points of view – guahua, guaxu and ideology. First, proving that the numerical symbols can not be replaced with gua at the Zhouyi. Also, yizhan(易占) using the numerical symbols had been coexisted with the Zhouyi which is using the two symbols – ‘’ and ‘ㅡ’ until the Warring States period. Second, it can be found at the Shangbochujian(上博楚簡) Zhouyi, Mawangdui Zhouyi, Qinghuajian(淸華簡) Biegua(別卦), Wangjiatai(王家臺) Guicang(歸藏). That there were two types of guaxu(卦序) of the Zhouyi at the Warring States period. It seems that these two types of guaxu(卦序) were merged and passed after the Han Dynasty. Third, it has been proved that Tuanzhuan(彖傳) had been made by Confucian by analyzing that Mawangdui Boshi through historical research.

Consequently, the hexagram names of Q1 appear to be more intentional, systematic, distinguishable, and stable across its various transmitting lines. Despite some textual differences, such as loan and variant characters, the hexagram names from various sources have maintained consistency along a single transmitting line. The Zhouyi's hexagram names found on Shanghai Museum bamboo slips should be older than those on the Mawangdui silk manuscripts, Shuangqudui bamboo strips, wooden strips discovered from the tomb of the Marquis of Haihun, and the received version. The names of their hexagrams varied primarily because they were passed down through different lineages. It is also interesting to note the similarities between the hexagram names of the Zhouyi Q1 and Guicang Q2 lineages. For example, the hexagram names of the Zhouyi found in the Mawangdui silk manuscripts, Shuangqudui bamboo strips, and wooden strips discovered from the tomb of the Marquis of Haihun align closely with those of the received Zhouyi. Furthermore, some of the hexagram names closely resemble those found in the Biegua from the Tsinghua bamboo slips and the Guicang from the Shuangqudui bamboo strips. The Zhouyi from the Mawangdui silk manuscripts and Shuangqudui bamboo strips were recorded during the reign of the Han emperor Wen 文 (r. 180–157 BCE), which indicates that they were made before the later convergence of the various Yi systems. Therefore, they likely upheld the Zhouyi's form during the late Warring States period and throughout the Qin- Han era (He 2025: 21). Moreover, the hexagram names found in the Yizhan discovered from the tomb of the Marquis of Haihun derive from the earlier form of the Zhouyi before its finalization. Thus, it indicates a transitional stage during that period (Zhu 2020: 254–266).  

As far as the Guicang lineage Q2 is concerned, it appears that its hexagram names may have originated from the ancient Zhouyi's hexagram names.

Additionally, the hexagram names of Q2 reflect various naming conventions from earlier times, suggesting that they are relatively old. Specifically, the hexagram names found in the Shifa and Biegua from the Tsinghua bamboo slips are likely older than those in the Wangjiatai bamboo strips and the recollected Guicang. A plausible explanation for the hexagram names of the Guicang lineage Q2 is that they may have been copied from the hexagram names used in the early Zhouyi lineage Q1 and then evolved independently through different transmission lines. Consequently, the hexagram names of the Guicang from the Shuanggudui bamboo strips and the recollected Guicang generally correspond to those in the received Zhouyi, although there are some notable differences. The hexagram names in the recollected Guicang show textual affinities of both the Guicang Q2 and Zhouyi Q1 lineages. The similarities in hexagram names across various Yi lineages highlight the complex origins and transmission of these names, likely due to the convergence of Yi systems in the early Western Han period (He 2025: 31- 32).  

## Stage Three: The completion of the Zhouyi and Guicang  

In the first two stages, this chapter has examined how the Zhouyi and Guicang originated from a single source: an early Yi system known as Q. Over time, they developed into two distinct divination systems: the Zhouyi Q1 and Guicang Q2 lineages. In this third stage, this chapter will discuss how the final versions of the Zhouyi Q1 and Guicang Q2 lineages evolved from those earlier manuscripts. Two charts in Appendix I show that the received Zhouyi and the recollected Guicang represent final versions. Notably, the final version of the Guicang lineage Q2 combined the textual constituents from the Zhouyi lineage Q1.  

The Zhouyi lineage Q1 was largely finalized during the reigns of the Han emperors Wu and Xuan. Therefore, the received Zhouyi should be considered the final version from Q1's transmitting line. This assumption is primarily based on the fact that the Yi system, established by the prominent master Tian He, became the orthodox

results.summary:
For this reason, we are missing most of the cultural background and other essential information concerning these texts. \(^{2}\) Nevertheless, this discovery still represents a great step forward in the understanding of the early developments of the Zhouyi. The manuscript, edited by Pu Maozuo 濮茅左, comprises only fifty- eight slips, corresponding to just about 36% (thirty- four hexagrams in total) of the received Zhouyi. \(^{3}\) From a structural standpoint, this manuscript is very similar to the Fuyang version: the hexagram picture, which is visually divided into two trigrams, is located at the top of the slip. As we shall see, this aspect is also present in the Shifa manuscript, which hypothetically belongs to the same cultural

area (the State of Chu) and the same historical period (mid- to late \(4^{\text{th}}\) century BCE).<sup>1</sup> The hexagram picture is immediately followed by the hexagram name—although with several graphic and lexical variants typical of the Chu script—the hexagram statement and the line statement. A few mysterious symbols are interpolated between these parts of the texts. Scholars have used them to reconstruct the hexagram sequence. I shall not delve too much into the details of this process. For the purposes of the present discussion, suffice it to say that, apparently, the sequence of the Shanghai Museum might be the same as the received one.<sup>2</sup>  

The last manuscript version was exhumed from the grave of the Marquis of Haihun 海昏侯 (Nanchang 南昌, Jiangxi 江西) in 2015. Among many grave goods belonging to the tomb occupant, a large corpus of manuscripts has been found, including yet another version of the Zhouyi which also dates to the beginning of the Western Han period. The text is written on sixty- four strips (i.e. one hexagram per each strip), and while the hexagram sequence is the same as the received one, the text following each hexagram is remarkably different.<sup>3</sup> One aspect which is worth mentioning as it is relevant to our discussion of the shuzi gua is that the hexagram pictures are not written with numbers (1 and 8) but with the more common broken and unbroken lines. This once again proves that the hexagram pictures were not visually standardised until the early Western Han.  

Finally, it is worth mentioning one last manuscript. In 1993, in the village of Wangjiatai 王家台, Hubei 湖北, inside the Tomb 15 (one of the sixteen tombs opened by some workers while digging a fish pond) archaeologists found a set of mantic tools, such as dice, wooden diviner's board, bamboo

sorting stalks, as well as the only authentic pre- imperial version of the Guicang, a different divination manual long thought to be lost, or regarded as a late forgery.  

Another somewhat related manuscript comes from the collection of looted texts purchased by Tsinghua University, called by the editors Biegua别卦 (Hexagrams). This manuscript consists of the hexagram sequence without text attached to each hexagram picture. The sequence is the same as the one found in the Mawangdui manuscript; however, for some reason the scribe(s) decided to write only the upper trigrams. Interestingly, unlike the other manuscript versions of the Zhouyi, the so- called broken line is written with the number 6 and not 8. Therefore, on this aspect, it bears a resemblance with the Shifa manuscript, which I shall discuss later in this chapter, as well as the dagger- axe which probably dates to the late Western Zhou period (see my Analytical Map for more details on this object). Lastly, the hexagrams names are also quite different.  

What can we gain from the analysis of these manuscripts? To be sure, different traditions which differed mainly in the way they depicted the broken line (either using 6 or 8), the hexagram and trigram order, as well as the names of the hexagrams coexisted until the mid \(2^{\text{nd}}\) century BCE. The text attached to each hexagram, when present, is quite consistent with the received tradition, and achieved its definitive shape by no later than the 300 BCE. Most importantly, the moral- philosophical aspect and the divinatory ones were still present until at least the early Western Han. The Fuyang manuscript in particular ‘confirms that the Zhouyi developed in the context of divination’ and the ‘humanistic rationale’ was attached to it much later than the orthodox exegetic tradition had claimed for centuries. Furthermore, Edward Shaughnessy, in his study on the unearthed Changes, remarks that the text was widespread in different kingdoms of the Warring

## Bamboo and Silk  

Associate Editors: Rens Krijgsman, Jing Liang, and Adam Schwartz Editors- in- Chief: Wei Chen and Edward L. Shaughnessy  

2025 Impact Factor: 0.3 5 Year Impact Factor: 0.4  

This is a Diamond Open Access journal. Articles are published in Open Access at no cost to the author.  

Bamboo and Silk is a peer- reviewed academic journal sponsored by the Center of Bamboo and Silk Manuscripts of Wuhan University. Based on unearthed Chinese bamboo and silk manuscripts from the Warring States period (476- 221 BC) and Qin (221- 206 BC), Han (206 BC- 220 AD), Wei (220- 265 AD) and Jin (265- 420 AD) Dynasties, this journal focuses on studies of character identification and textual reconstitution, and studies of the social, political, economic and legal systems as well as ideology, culture, language, customs and other aspects reflected by these manuscripts. The journal includes research articles on bamboo and silk manuscripts and book reviews. All articles are peer reviewed by anonymous outside experts as well as by the editorial board, and reflect the current state of international academic research issues on Chinese bamboo and silk manuscripts.  

Bamboo and Silk is primarily based on Jian Bo 简帛, a Chinese journal that was initially published in 2006 by Shanghai Chinese Classics Publishing House Co., Ltd., with some articles chosen from Jian Bo 简帛 and translated into English. The journal accepts submissions in English as well.  

Bamboo and Silk is indexed by Web of Science.  

Order information: +44 330 333 0049 | customerservices@brill.com Submission information: brill.com/authors

『주역』은 도대체 언제 유가의 경전이 되었는가? 곽점초간과 마왕퇴 백서주역 등의 발견은 통행본 주역이 전국 중기 이후에 이루어졌거나, 『역』은 분서 이후의 진한시기에 비로소 유가 경전이 되었다는 관점을 무너뜨린다. 유가가 『역』을 경전으로 보는 이유는 그것을 철학적 의미가 담겨있는 책으로 보기 때문이다.『역』이 유가의 경전에 포함된 것은 공자에 의한 것이고, 『주역』의 유가 경전화의 과정은 공자의 “晩而喜易”에서 시작한다. 『주역』은 더 이상 점서가 아니라, 성인의 말을 담은 책으로, 마침내 유가의 경전 속에 진입하게 된다. 이로부터 유가들은 『주역』을 해석할 때 占筮가 아니라 德義를 찾는데 최선의 노력을 기울인다.

When did Zhouyi become Confucian Classic? Manuscripts of the Chu bamboo slips from Guodian and Mawangdui silk manuscript banished the assertion such as the received version of Zhouyi was formulated after the mid of Warring States period and the Zhouyi was enshrined as a Confucian classic till the turn of the Qin and Han dynasties even in the Western Han dynasty. The reason why Confucian school regarded the Yi as a classic was that the quality of the Yi was thought to be a book of philosophical significance. Yi was entered six classics by Confucius, because he changed viewpoint of Zhouyi. In later life, Confucius begun to develop a liking for the Zhouy. Zhouyi was seen as a book of recoding the words of the saint by the Confucians, instead of a book of divination, so they tried their best to find the morallity and wisdom in the process of interpreting Zhouyi.
